summary: Ethical problems of hacking, protecting data from unauthorised access, problems caused by malware, and what privacy policies contain.

theory.title: Ethical problems of computer system cracking

blocks.content: Gaining **unauthorised access** to a computer system or data, usually by exploiting weaknesses or stolen passwords.

items.title: Black-hat hacker
items.content: Breaks in illegally for profit, damage or spying.

items.title: White-hat (ethical) hacker
items.content: Tests systems **with permission** (penetration testing) to find and fix weaknesses.

items.title: Grey-hat hacker
items.content: Breaks in without permission but without malicious intent — still illegal.

blocks.title: Ethical and social problems
rows: Personal messages, photos and medical data are exposed
Money, identities, intellectual property and trade secrets are stolen
Data deleted or altered; hospitals, banks or schools cannot work
Customers stop using an organisation that was hacked
Who pays for the damage? Was the organisation negligent in protecting data?
Is exposing a vulnerability without permission ethical if it helps fix it?
Unauthorised access is a **criminal offence** (Criminal Code of the Republic of Kazakhstan; similar laws worldwide)

items.title: Strong passwords and policies
items.content: At least 12 characters, a mix of letters, digits and symbols; not reused; changed after a breach; account lock-out after failed attempts.

items.title: Two-factor authentication
items.content: Password plus a code from a phone or a security key.

items.title: Access rights (permissions)
items.content: Users get only the **privileges they need** (read, write, delete); students cannot change marks.

items.title: Encryption
items.content: Data on disks and in transfer (HTTPS, VPN) cannot be read if intercepted.

items.title: Firewalls and updates
items.content: Block unauthorised network access and close known security holes.

items.title: Physical security and monitoring
items.content: Locked rooms, logging out, screen locks, **audit logs** of who accessed what.

blocks.content: Use the scenario: "The school should give teachers **write access** to marks and students **read-only access**, so students cannot change their grades."

rows: Hospitals and businesses stop working; ransom payments fund crime
Industrial espionage; leaked customer data → fines
Networks overloaded; cost of cleaning and downtime
Used in DDoS attacks against websites and e-government services

blocks.content: A public statement by a website, app or organisation explaining **what personal data it collects, why, how it is used, stored and protected, who it is shared with, and what rights the user has**.

blocks.title: What a privacy policy should contain
rows: Name, email, location, browsing history, cookies
To provide the service, improve it, send newsletters, show adverts
With payment providers, advertisers, government when required by law
Where data is stored, for how long, how it is protected (encryption)
See, correct, download or delete your data; withdraw consent; opt out of marketing
Which cookies are used and how to refuse them
How to contact the data protection officer

blocks.content: Many users accept privacy policies **without reading them** — they may agree to their data being sold or shared. Children's data needs special protection and parental consent.
